name: Sheep placenta injection

card.summary: Injected or topical placental extract, often sheep-derived or Laennec-style human placenta hydrolysate, used by some people as a skin rejuvenation and glow treatment.
card.aka: placenta extract injection; Laennec-style placental extract
card.note: Animal-derived extracts have been described as containing hormones, and regulators have cautioned about placenta extracts; products and injections vary in regulatory status by country.

quick.overview:
Placental extracts are products made from animal or human placenta. Sheep placenta is the most common animal source in skin and hair products, and in some beauty clinics extracts are given as injections in the hope of brighter, fresher-looking skin. People who use them describe the aim as skin rejuvenation and a healthier complexion.

Human placenta hydrolysate (Laennec) and similar products are registered as drugs in some countries for liver disease and menopausal symptoms, and trials listed for them cover liver disease and shoulder problems rather than skin appearance. Published research on sheep placenta for skin is limited.
quick.how: Descriptions of use are of clinic-administered injections or of creams, serums and ampoules containing extract, usually repeated as a series of sessions. This article does not cover dosing or sourcing; products vary widely in origin and processing.
quick.risks: Descriptions of placenta extracts note that they may contain hormones such as estrogen and progesterone. A 1998 case report described girls developing breast or pubic hair after using hair products containing placenta or estrogen, which resolved on stopping. The FDA is reported to have stated that placenta extracts may be hazardous, and injectables carry the general risks of injection such as infection or allergic reaction. Regulatory status differs by country.

lead: Sheep placenta injection refers to the use of extracts of sheep placenta, delivered by injection in some beauty and wellness settings, for skin rejuvenation. It sits within a wider family of placental extracts that includes human placenta preparations such as Laennec and Melsmon.[1][2]

People who use placental extracts for appearance describe improved skin brightness, texture and a fresher complexion. Sheep is described as the most common animal source for hair and skin treatments, and the extracts are said to supply protein and hormones such as estrogen and progesterone.[1]

Published clinical research on placenta extracts concentrates on other uses. Registered trials of Laennec human placenta hydrolysate involve chronic liver disease and shoulder impingement, and a rat study examined a human placenta preparation injected at an acupuncture point in arthritis.[3][4][5]

chain: Placental extract is injected or applied to skin
Believers cite proteins, growth factors and hormones in the extract
Skin is described as brighter, smoother or firmer
angle.text: Users report using placental extracts for a brighter, smoother-looking complexion. The mechanism offered is that extract supplies proteins and hormones to skin, which is a proponent claim not established in published skin trials.

infobox: Varies by country; some human placenta products are registered drugs

paras: Placenta extracts are used in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals in some cultures; companies sell hair and skin treatments containing animal placenta extract, most commonly from sheep.[1] Human placenta extracts include Melsmon, produced by a Japanese company that has operated since 1956 and used for menopause, and Laennec, prescribed for chronic hepatitis.[1] Placentrex is an Indian injectable made from fresh human placenta.[1]

Proponents of placental extract treatments present them as a skin rejuvenation option, with the extract described as supplying protein and hormones.[1] Sheep-derived products appear in creams, ampoules and, in some clinics, injection programs.

The FDA is reported to say that placenta extract may be hazardous, with some products carrying restrictions and warnings.[1] A 1998 report described four girls aged 1 to 8 who developed breast tissue or pubic hair after using hair products containing estrogen or placenta extract; the changes reversed after stopping.[1]
Reviews of ingesting human placenta note a CDC report of infection in a newborn linked to placenta capsules, which is a separate practice.[6]

No studies found for sheep placenta injections for skin appearance. Related research includes registered trials of Laennec human placenta hydrolysate in chronic liver disease and in shoulder impingement injection, and a rat arthritis study of a human placenta preparation.[3][4][5]

timeline.event: Melsmon Pharmaceutical begins operating in Japan, producing human placenta extract.[1]
A pediatric case report links hair products containing placenta extract or estrogen to early breast and pubic hair development.[1]
